CausalChain: Gut microbiota converts primary bile acids into LCA -> LCA physiologically accumulates in breast tissue -> LCA binds and activates TGR5 on TAMs -> TGR5 activation triggers cAMP/PKA signaling and NF-κB modulation -> This signaling cascade reprograms TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 to an immunostimulatory M1 phenotype -> Enhanced M1 activity increases immune surveillance and tumor cell apoptosis -> Elevated antitumor immunity improves response to chemotherapy, with nanodelivery and omics validation added
Hypothesis: At physiological concentrations present in breast tissue, lithocholic acid activates the TGR5 receptor on tumor-associated macrophages, triggering a cAMP/PKA and NF-κB signaling cascade that repolarizes these cells from a pro-tumor (M2) phenotype to an anti-tumor (M1) phenotype. This macrophage repolarization enhances immune surveillance and tumor cell apoptosis, thereby suppressing breast cancer progression and potentiating the effects of chemotherapy. Furthermore, we propose that modern nanotechnology-based targeted delivery of LCA and high-resolution omics technologies will refine our understanding and amplify the therapeutic utility of this mechanism.
Abstract: We propose that physiological levels of lithocholic acid (LCA) in breast tissue, derived from gut microbial metabolism of primary bile acids, activate TGR5 receptors on tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) to reprogram them from a pro-tumor M2 phenotype to an antitumor M1 state. Activation of TGR5 triggers a cAMP/PKA signaling cascade that modulates NF-κB pathways, ultimately enhancing immune surveillance and promoting apoptosis of tumor cells. In addition, we hypothesize that contemporary nanodelivery systems can be utilized to optimize LCA bioavailability at the tumor site, while advanced omics techniques (transcriptomics and proteomics) can elucidate the detailed signaling mechanisms underlying macrophage repolarization. This integrative approach not only reinforces the mechanistic link between bile acid physiology and cancer immunomodulation but also outlines a practical framework for improving chemotherapeutic efficacy in breast cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that physiological LCA levels activate TGR5 on TAMs to shift them from M2 to M1, enhancing chemotherapy outcomes. The revised hypothesis builds on this by explicitly integrating advanced nanodelivery systems to ensure LCA reaches effective concentrations in breast tissue and incorporates contemporary omics approaches to detail the underlying molecular mechanisms. Additionally, the revised version emphasizes the complete causal chain—from microbial conversion of bile acids to the final enhancement of chemo-sensitivity—thereby strengthening both the scientific rationale and the practical applicability of the hypothesis.
